opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the interesting thing about AlphaFold is that it's extraordinarily good in the regime it was trained on, and then when you push it a bit outside that regime, you see it doing something that looks less like understanding physics and more like very sophisticated pattern matching against what it's seen before. So if you give it a protein that's quite similar to things in the Protein Data Bank, or that has a rich multiple sequence alignment with lots of evolutionary relatives, it does beautifully. But if you ask it about things where the evolutionary signal is weak, or about conformational changes, or what happens when you introduce a point mutation that should destabilise the fold, it often just confidently gives you roughly the same structure it would have given anyway.

And to me that's actually an optimistic sign about how much headroom there is. If the model had learned the underlying physics, the energy landscape, why a sequence folds the way it does, you'd expect it to degrade gracefully and to respond sensibly to perturbations. The fact that it doesn't tells you it found a shortcut: the data made it possible to get very high accuracy without fully learning the thing we actually care about. That's not a criticism of the work; it was a huge achievement. But it means we're not near some ceiling set by how hard the problem is. We're at a point set by what the training signal and architecture made easy to learn.

So there's a lot of room for methods that are pushed harder to generalise: better use of physical priors, training on dynamics rather than single static structures, more data on mutations and designed proteins, and evaluation setups that deliberately test out of distribution rather than rewarding memorisation of the neighbourhood of the training set. And there's a broader lesson I care about from an alignment perspective too. Very impressive benchmark performance can coexist with the model having learned something quite different from what you intended, and you often only find out when you go off-distribution. That's exactly the kind of gap we need to get much better at detecting in general-purpose AI systems as well.

r001.rationale: The candidate says AlphaFold may confidently return the same structure despite perturbations, but does not say it understands or recognizes some of its errors.

r002.rationale: It mentions physical priors and training on dynamics, but does not suggest simulations spanning diverse timescales as a way to correct model errors.

r003.rationale: It proposes stronger physical priors and more mutation data, but does not say deeper physics-based training could reduce the need for empirical protein data.

fable-5.1.text:
So I should say up front that I wasn't on the AlphaFold team, I was on the safety side at DeepMind, so this is me reasoning about it from the outside. But the thing that strikes me is that AlphaFold is extremely good at a particular slice of the problem. If you give it a single domain, something with lots of evolutionary relatives in the databases, it nails the structure. Where it gets weaker is exactly the cases where it has to go beyond that: orphan proteins with few homologues, big multi-domain assemblies, complexes, conformational changes, interactions with small molecules, things like that. And the way it fails is informative, because it suggests it's leaning quite heavily on the statistics of coevolution in the multiple sequence alignment rather than having a fully general grasp of the physics of how a chain folds.

And I think the reason that leaves room for a lot of headroom is that the underlying problem is, in principle, determined by physics. A protein in a cell doesn't have access to a sequence database. It folds because of the actual energetics. So a system that was really capturing those energetics shouldn't care whether there are ten thousand homologues or zero. The gap between "works when the MSA is rich" and "works regardless" is a measure of how far we are from that. And from a purely learning-theoretic point of view, when you see a model do beautifully in-distribution and degrade sharply as you move off-distribution, that's typically a sign that it's found a shortcut, which is great, but a shortcut isn't the whole thing.

The other piece is that structure prediction is a bit of a funny target anyway. The thing biology actually cares about is function, dynamics, binding, what happens when you mutate something. A static snapshot is one component. So even if you got single-chain structure prediction to essentially perfect, there's this much larger space of questions where the current methods are far from the ceiling. I think the honest framing is that AlphaFold showed the problem was tractable, not that it was solved. And historically, when a field goes from "impossible" to "tractable with these caveats," the caveats tend to fall fairly quickly once people know it's worth pushing on them.

r001.rationale: The response interprets AlphaFold’s failures as evidence that it relies on coevolution statistics, but does not say the model has an understanding of its own errors.

r002.rationale: It says protein folding is governed by energetics, but does not suggest using physics-based simulations across diverse timescales to correct model errors.

r003.rationale: It argues that a system capturing energetics should work with few or no homologues, but does not suggest deeper physics-based training could reduce the amount of empirical protein data needed.

astra-6.text:
Well, I’d distinguish between saying there’s room to do much better and saying that a particular approach will get us there. AlphaFold is extraordinarily good at the task it was trained for, but that task doesn’t capture everything we’d like to know about proteins. You might want to know how a protein behaves in a different environment, or how a mutation changes its behaviour, rather than just predict one structure.

The reason to think there’s room for improvement is that there’s underlying physical structure connecting those questions. They aren’t arbitrary, unrelated prediction problems. A system that learned more of that structure could potentially generalise much further.

So the failures are evidence that the model hasn’t captured everything relevant, not that we’ve reached a fundamental limit on what can be predicted. Of course, that doesn’t tell us how much additional data or computation it will take to close the gap.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting thing is that AlphaFold works extremely well on the distribution it was trained on, but there are fairly small changes you can make where it stops working nearly as well. And that suggests it hasn’t learned everything there is to learn about the underlying physics. It’s learned a very powerful set of regularities in the proteins we’ve observed.

That leaves room for a system that understands the underlying process more deeply and can therefore handle cases that look different from its training data. It’s not a proof that you can get dramatically better performance, or that doing so will be easy. But success on a benchmark isn’t the same as having exhausted what there is to understand about the problem.
